title: How sure are we?
lead: Its behaviour was first reported in the scientific literature in 2001, and the species was formally named in 2005. It lives on open sand and mud, is hard to find, and has been studied far less than its fame suggests. This page tries to separate what has been recorded from what is repeated.

A.description: Directly observed and described in peer-reviewed literature, with the posture and movement recorded.

B.description: Reported in the scientific literature, but with reservations: few observations, cautious wording by the authors, or little descriptive detail.

C.description: Popular or anecdotal claim. No peer-reviewed description was found during research for this project.

limitations.heading: What the 3D model is, and is not

procedural.title: The octopus is procedural and schematic
procedural.text: The body, arms, web and suckers are generated by code from simple curves and profiles. Proportions follow published measurements where they exist (arms at least 6.5 times the mantle length), but this is not a scan or a sculpt of a real animal.

internal.title: Internal anatomy is generalised
internal.text: The internal organs of the mimic octopus have barely been described. Organ shapes and positions are simplified from the general octopus body plan, mostly from the common octopus, Octopus vulgaris.

inkSac.title: The ink sac is unconfirmed for this species
inkSac.text: Most shallow-water octopuses have an ink sac, but no source read for this project states whether Thaumoctopus mimicus has one. It is shown as part of the general body plan and labelled as unconfirmed.

diagrams.title: Skin and nerves are diagrams
diagrams.text: The skin block is not to scale and its layers come from other cephalopods. The glowing nerve signals show the order in which parts are involved, not real conduction speeds.

curves.title: Arms are driven by curves, not muscles
curves.text: Arm shapes are produced by a mathematical curve with a handful of parameters. They illustrate what a muscular hydrostat can do; they are not a simulation of muscle.

timing.title: Animation timing is illustrative
timing.text: Transformations are slowed and split into stages (arms, body, skin, movement) so they can be followed. A real animal changes all of these together and far faster. No swimming speeds have been published.

referenceAnimals.title: Reference animals are simplified
referenceAnimals.text: The ten comparison animals are low-detail models built for silhouette and pattern only. They do not represent particular species unless one is named.

colours.title: Colours are approximate
colours.text: Colour was matched by eye to published descriptions (brown and white bands), not measured. Octopuses are thought to be colour-blind, and how the pattern appears to a predator is unknown.

references.heading: References
references.note: Each entry notes how much of the source was actually read while preparing this site. Several key papers could only be read as abstracts; statements that rest on them are worded accordingly.
